name: Skin whitening/bleaching

image.caption: Sweet Georgia Brown skin bleaching cream advertisement 1930s

lead: Skin whitening, also called lightening or bleaching, uses chemical agents to reduce melanin so skin looks lighter and more even. People use it to fade dark spots, brighten the complexion and lift overall tone, and some looksmaxxing posters say it raises their rating by roughly 0.5 to 1 PSL.

Most lightening agents inhibit tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production; others block melanin transfer to skin cells or destroy melanocytes. Glutathione is reported to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin toward its lighter form. Agents such as hydroquinone, arbutin and kojic acid have been studied for pigmentation disorders, and the practice itself dates back more than two thousand years.

paras: People use topical creams and serums, oral supplements, or clinic-administered injections, usually as a routine over weeks to months, often alongside sunscreen and general skincare. Results show gradually as existing pigment fades and new pigment production is reduced.

Reported harms include mercury toxicity from contaminated products, skin thinning from long-term steroid creams, ochronosis and contact dermatitis from hydroquinone, and serious reactions from intravenous glutathione. Skin becomes more sun-sensitive. Many products are restricted or banned in several countries, and regulators and dermatology reviews document these problems.

angle.text: Users apply or take lightening agents to reduce melanin, fading dark spots and lifting overall skin tone for a brighter, more even complexion. Some forum posters say it raises their rating by about 0.5 to 1 PSL. Topical agents such as hydroquinone and arbutin have been studied clinically for pigmentation.

lead: Skin whitening, also called skin lightening or bleaching, is the use of chemical substances to lighten skin color or even out tone by reducing melanin. Recorded practices date back more than two thousand years, and use is widespread across Africa, Asia and elsewhere. [1]

A 2022 dermatology review describes cosmetic skin lightening as a growing public health problem among communities of color, with well-documented adverse health effects alongside social and cultural drivers. [2] Reviews of the agents themselves, such as glutathione, describe a gap between popular use and evidence of efficacy and safety. [3]

On looksmax.org the topic is discussed by some users as a looksmaxxing tactic, often alongside ethnicity and the PSL rating scale; posts include claims that lightening adds to a rating and recommendations of particular products. [4]
infobox: Hydroquinone, kojic acid, glutathione, corticosteroids, mercury (illicit)
Hydroquinone, tretinoin and corticosteroids banned in cosmetics [1]

paras: Agents range from topical creams to oral supplements and injections. Wikipedia lists hydroquinone, kojic acid, alpha hydroxy acids, tretinoin, corticosteroids such as clobetasol, glutathione and inorganic mercury among the substances used, and notes that some are effective while others are toxic or of questionable safety. [1] A medicinal chemistry review describes tyrosinase inhibitors as the main route of drug development. [5]

Wikipedia traces lightening practices to antiquity in Egypt, Greece and East Asia, and to lead-based preparations in Elizabethan Europe, with commercial products marketed in the 19th and 20th centuries United States. [1] It reports usage figures from a 2013 source of 77% of Nigerian women, 52% of Senegalese women and 25% of Malian women, and describes motivations including associations of lighter skin with beauty, status and marriage prospects, as well as treatment of pigmentation conditions. [1]

Critics cited in the same article say the practice reinforces colorism, while the dermatology review frames it as a practice with sociocultural implications that clinicians should discuss sensitively with patients. [1][2]

A 2016 review of glutathione as a skin-lightening agent found a dichotomy between popularity and evidence, noting that no evidence supports the efficacy of intravenous injections and that adverse effects led the Philippine FDA to issue warnings. [3] A 2025 narrative review reported significant but variable melanin reductions with oral glutathione and good-level reductions with topical forms of varying sustainability, while describing intravenous use as associated with serious safety concerns such as anaphylaxis and hepatotoxicity and calling for large, rigorous trials.
Wikipedia states that the effectiveness of glutathione was unclear as of 2019, and that kojic acid has been reported as effective in some studies. [1]

Clinical evidence consists mainly of reviews and small trials of individual agents, chiefly glutathione, examined for melasma and other pigmentation uses or skin tone. [3] No studies found that test whether lightening skin changes attractiveness ratings or dating outcomes, the claim made in forum threads. [4]

Wikipedia lists mercury toxicity (neurological and kidney damage), hydroquinone-linked ochronosis, cataracts and dermatitis, and long-term corticosteroid effects such as skin atrophy and glaucoma, along with greater sun sensitivity and infection risk. [1] It also reports that many such products are illegal in various countries yet remain on sale, with weak enforcement. [1]
Reviews also describe serious adverse events associated with intravenous glutathione. [3]

A looksmax.org thread on the subject opens by saying lightening adds half a point to a full point of PSL and lists groups the poster thinks it applies to, products such as kojic acid soap and video channels; replies dispute whether lighter skin is desirable. [4] No published study has evaluated the PSL scale or such claimed gains.

lore.intro: Skin lightening is discussed on looksmax.org as a method to change one's rating or ethnic appearance, with debate over whether lighter skin is more attractive. [4]
